keep: The example winding's readings scatter round R = 0.04T + 10, the same law as lesson 5's winding, so the lesson picks up exactly where lesson 5's ignores panel left off ('real readings scatter a little around one').
No reading sits on the laid line, so 'it need not pass through any reading' is visible, and the count is four above and four below, which is SERC's rule [1].
The spring is the right contrast for the through-zero pin: there the physics puts the line through the origin [2], while the winding has resistance at 0 °C.
The analogy (the middle of a wavering needle's swing) is from the trade and is new to the course.
fix: False absolute: 'Real readings scatter, so they never sit exactly on one line' is untrue (a reading can land on the line). Say they scatter a little, so they seldom sit exactly on one line.

False absolute and causal step skipped: 'Do not force the line through zero' is wrong for the spring, which the same paragraph says goes through zero. The rule is: pin it only when the physics says y is 0 when x is 0. And it never shows why a pinned line is wrong for the winding: with the pin at (0, 0) the line can only swing, so at R = 0.26T the sticks grow to 7.9 Ω at 10 °C and 7.5 Ω at 80 °C, and every reading above sits on the left, every one below on the right.

The count is taught as the whole rule. The pinned line R = 0.26T also splits the readings four and four, so the count alone passes a bad line. Teach the count as a check alongside short sticks and the above and below readings spread along the line, not bunched at the ends; a pattern means the line is tilted.

Causal step skipped on the gradient: why from the line and why far apart. Show the neighbouring-readings slip with its numbers (0.8 Ω ÷ 10 °C = 0.08, because each reading carries its own scatter of up to 0.2 Ω and over 10 °C the scatter is as big as the rise), and the far-apart reason (reading heights off the line to within about 0.1 Ω changes a 0.4 Ω rise by half but a 2.0 Ω rise by a tenth).
c is never worked out in the text: show c = 10.8 − 0.04 × 20 = 10.0 Ω, and catch the slip of taking the first reading (10.5 Ω at 10 °C) as c.

The spring is talked about, not taught: give its readings, the straight part's line F = 2.5x from (0, 0) and (12, 30), 2.5 N per mm, and what the last two readings give (0.9 N per mm) if used. Keep [2]'s qualifier: the graph is straight provided the limit is not exceeded; the quote does not say what happens past it, so say these example readings bend there.

The interactive's whatAmILookingAt names no screens, no puzzles, no hints and no step-by-step reasons, and its numbers list misses most numbers the screens will show (sticks, the pin's 0.26, the spring and machine readings, the puzzle options). The builder cannot build twelve screens from it.

ignores is thin: it should say the sticks are measured straight up and down in Ω, the eye fit is one of many acceptable lines, the readings are made up and the pinned line's 0.26 is the interactive's choice; and that the calculated fit (least squares) comes at college.

Analogy breaks is too thin to teach: say specifically that a needle has no tilt to get wrong, while a line must get its height and its slope right at once, so it can split the readings evenly and still be tilted.

Practice is a list of names, not usable: give the full worked example (line points, gradient, c, law, a check with an unused reading) and show each mistake failing with numbers (5 readings above 1 below; 7.7 ÷ 60 through zero; 0.5 ÷ 10 from neighbouring readings).

Missing the course puzzle's sentence in its own right, the forward pointers (curved laws straightened with logs in Exponentials and logarithms; least squares calculated at college) and the y = ax + b form [11] Dan's college syllabus uses.
